name: Short-Form Claim Hook
use_when: A short-form video needs an immediate reason to stop scrolling.
The source idea can be framed as a strong desire, social proof, controversy, surprise, or disbelief.
The agent is planning the first five seconds before editing motion and captions.
avoid_when: The claim cannot be supported by the video.
The topic is sensitive and controversy would cheapen or misrepresent it.
The user wants a calm brand-safe educational style where an aggressive claim would break trust.

timeline_pattern.claim_types: Use big desire, social proof, controversy, surprising result, or a question that makes viewers ask how it is possible.
timeline_pattern.research_rule: Use trend research or niche-specific AI prompts; generic idea prompts usually produce weak hooks.
timeline_pattern.promise_rule: The hook must set up a payoff the rest of the short actually delivers.

motion.rule: Support the claim with a clear face, result, proof frame, or readable text; do not obscure the hook with random effects.

sound.rule: Opening voice should start cleanly and energetically. Music or SFX can lift the hook but must not mask the claim.

captions.rule: The first caption should clarify the claim at phone size and should not cover the face or proof.

color.rule: The first frame should be bright and legible enough for the subject, result, or proof to register.

implementation.ffmpeg: Render the first five seconds as a separate review clip. Use waveform inspection to remove pre-hook silence and contact sheets to check first-frame clarity.
implementation.remotion: Represent hook data with claimType, claimText, proofFrame, hookEndFrame, and payoffFrame so the promise can be checked later.
implementation.blender: Use animated claim text only when it makes the promise faster to understand than live footage alone.
implementation.capcut_equivalent: Start with the strongest claim or proof, trim opening silence, add readable first-line captions, and preview at phone size.
implementation.premiere_equivalent: Place markers for claim, proof, context, and payoff. Review the first five seconds before polishing the rest of the short.

common_mistakes: Using a generic idea prompt and ending with a weak claim.
Opening with setup before the attractive claim.
Making a controversial claim the video cannot support.
Using energy, captions, or effects to hide that the hook has no real payoff.
qc: Can a cold viewer understand the claim within five seconds?
Is the claim supported by proof or payoff later in the short?
Does the hook avoid unsupported controversy or exaggeration?
Is the first caption or visual proof readable at phone size?
Does the opening audio start cleanly without masking the claim?
